text: By and large, yes. Many people click 'accept' without reading terms, or post details like their location without a second thought. The trouble is that data can be combined to build a surprisingly detailed profile, which may be used for targeted advertising or, worse, fraud. I think part of the solution is education, but companies should also be required to make privacy settings clear and strict by default.

text: Within limits. Companies have a legitimate interest in protecting confidential data, so some monitoring of work accounts is understandable. However, tracking every keystroke or private messages crosses the line, as it undermines trust and can damage morale. I'd say transparency is the key. If staff are told clearly what is monitored and why, most would accept it as a reasonable condition of the job.

text: It cuts both ways. On the one hand, tools that generate text or images can tempt people to skip the hard, messy part of creating something. On the other hand, they lower the barrier, so someone with no training can now bring an idea to life. I suspect creativity won't disappear but will shift, with originality lying more in the idea and the curation than in the technical execution.

text: I believe so, because a handful of firms now control information, advertising and even public debate, which is a lot of power without much accountability. Critics argue regulation stifles innovation, and there's some truth in that. Nevertheless, well-designed rules, such as protecting data or requiring fair competition, tend to encourage healthier markets rather than hinder them. The real difficulty is keeping legislation up to date with technology that changes so quickly.
